# One Command Surface, Two Dispatchers

Publish one vocabulary of verbs — `test`, `package`, `lint`, `shots`, `clean` — and implement it
twice: a `Makefile` for anyone with [[make]], and a PowerShell script with the same target names for
a Windows machine that has none. The documentation names the verb, never the runner.

## Why not pick one

Neither wins. `make` is absent from a default Windows install and the alternatives are a download;
PowerShell is not what a contributor on Linux reaches for. The projects here are developed on Windows
and published for everyone, so the choice is between excluding a machine, adding a task runner as a
dependency, or writing the second dispatcher — about eighty lines that never change.

The scripts are dispatchers, not build systems. The real work lives in `npm run`, `pytest`, `node
harness/…` and the Python entry points; both files only route to it. That keeps the duplication
shallow, which is the only reason it stays correct.

## The failure mode, and the guard

Two dispatchers drift: a target gets added to one and forgotten in the other, and the README's
instruction is now wrong for half its readers. [[agent-orchestrator]] closes that with a unit test —
`test_both_runners_offer_the_same_targets` parses the target names out of both files and asserts the
sets are equal ([[tests-that-guard-the-repository]]). Drift becomes a red test rather than a bug
report from the one contributor on the other OS.

This wiki's own tooling has the same shape (`Makefile` beside `brain.ps1`) and, at the time of
writing, no such guard.

## The nice second-order effect

Having to name every operation as a verb forces the operations to be *nameable*. A repository where
`make test` means the whole gate — and says how many checks that is — has already decided what "the
gate" is. That decision is more valuable than either script.
